items.title: Behavioral Intention Towards Artificial Intelligence Integration and Teachers’ Self-Efficacy
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has reshaped instructional practices, making teachers’ readiness and confidence critical considerations. This study determined the level of Grade 7 teachers’ behavioral intention towards AI integration and self-efficacy. Specifically, it described the respondents’ profile in terms of age, sex, position, educational attainment, and AI-related training; their behavioral intention based on attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control; their self-efficacy concerning student engagement, instructional strategy, and classroom management; the relationship between the two variables; and whether respondents’ profile moderates this relationship. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was employed, involving 185 Grade 7 teachers from the districts of Kadingilan, Damulog, Kibawe, and Dangcagan in the Division of Bukidnon, selected through universal sampling. Data were gathered using a researcher-made questionnaire. Mean, standard deviation, Pearson Product-Moment Correlation, and multiple linear regression were used for statistical treatment. Findings revealed a very high level of behavioral intention and self-efficacy among teachers, with a significant positive relationship between the two variables, further moderated by respondents’ profile, particularly position and trainings attended. The study concludes that teachers’ favorable behavioral intention toward AI strengthens their self-efficacy. It is recommended that school heads may enhance teachers’ readiness and confidence in integrating AI into instruction.

items.title: Can AI Assistants Trigger Mental Illness in Users?
items.abstract: As conversational artificial intelligence models become ubiquitous fixtures in professional and personal workflows, the nature of human-tool interaction has the potential to gradually shift from mechanical utility to parasocial dependency. While existing literature frequently addresses adverse events related to data privacy, algorithmic bias, and intellectual deskilling, the pathopsychological sequelae of sustained AI integration remain largely unexamined. Here, we describe and preliminarily characterize the AI Assistant Syndrome, a human psychiatric construct encompassing acute chatbot-induced anxiety and mental exhaustion. This preliminary description will guide future systematic investigations to recognize, prevent, and treat this syndrome.

items.title: Cognitive Engagement, Learning Strategies, Adjustment to College and Academic Motivation: A Structural Equation Model on Academic Success Among College Students
items.abstract: This study examined the relationships among cognitive engagement, learning strategies, adjustment to college, academic motivation, and academic success to determine the best-fit structural equation model among Bachelor of Elementary Education students in Region XIII (Caraga), Philippines. Anchored in Self-Regulated Learning Theory and Academic Adjustment Theory, the study employed a quantitative, non-experimental descriptive-correlational design involving 470 second-, third-, and fourth-year students from three state universities, selected through proportional stratified random sampling. Data were collected using five adapted, validated, and reliability-tested questionnaires and analyzed through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and structural equation modeling. Results revealed very high levels of cognitive engagement (M = 4.27), learning strategies (M = 4.32), college adjustment (M = 4.34), academic motivation (M = 4.32), and academic success (M = 4.31). All four predictors demonstrated significant positive correlations with academic success, with academic motivation exhibiting the strongest relationship (r = .519). The final structural model demonstrated excellent fit (CMIN/DF = .845, CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = .000) and explained 32.5% of the variance in academic success. Academic motivation (β = .270, p = .020) and learning strategies (β = .262, p = .017) emerged as significant direct predictors, whereas college adjustment and cognitive engagement showed nonsignificant direct effects. The findings emphasize the importance of strengthening academic motivation and effective learning strategies through learner-centered instruction and institutional support programs. The study supports Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by providing evidence to inform educational practices and student success initiatives. Its sustainability contribution lies in supporting evidence-based academic planning, student retention, and continuous improvement in higher education.

items.title: Comprehensive Analytical Study on Spatial Reasoning and Adaptation of Human Brain Versus Artificial Intelligence - A Review Report
items.abstract: Recent advances in computer vision, spatial computing, robotics, and embodied artificial intelligence (AI) have substantially improved machine capabilities in visual perception, navigation, spatial reasoning, and object manipulation. However, performance on structured benchmarks and controlled environments does not necessarily demonstrate equivalence to human spatial intelligence in complex real-world situations. This review examines whether current AI systems can reproduce the breadth and flexibility of human spatial and embodied intelligence, with particular emphasis on their implications for the potential replacement of humans by AI. The review synthesizes theoretical and empirical literature on human spatial cognition, embodied AI, vision-language-action models, robotics, and relevant AI capability benchmarks. The evidence is organised around four dimensions: (1) biological sensorimotor coupling and proprioception, (2) zero-shot spatial problem-solving and dynamic affordance recognition, (3) physical common-sense reasoning and adaptation, and (4) energy-efficient and context-sensitive spatial processing. Existing research indicates that AI systems have achieved considerable progress in perception, navigation, planning, and manipulation, but continue to encounter challenges involving unfamiliar environments, occlusion, uncertainty, dynamic obstacles, changing object configurations, physical interaction, long-horizon adaptation, and generalisation beyond training distributions. Human spatial intelligence, in contrast, integrates perception, proprioception, embodied experience, contextual knowledge, physical intuition, memory, and flexible real-time decision-making as an interconnected system. The reviewed evidence therefore suggests that current AI can augment and extend human spatial capabilities but cannot yet reproduce the breadth, adaptability, embodied experience, and contextual flexibility of human spatial intelligence. Spatial ability consequently represents an important dimension of human irreplaceability and supports a future paradigm of human–AI complementarity rather than complete human substitution.

items.title: Defining AGI: Solution/Abundance/Apocalypse/God
items.abstract: Artificial general intelligence (AGI) has changed from a scientific aim to a moving goalpost of industrial AI ambitions. As far as the AI industry is concerned, it is simultaneously the most consequential invention in human history and a manageable, iterative technology. But what is AGI, aside from a future promise? This paper identifies four rhetorical registers through which AGI is defined, in the words of those giving it shape. In doing so, we base ourselves on the AI industry’s own discussions of AGI, including the 2026 India AI Impact Summit, AI companies’ blog posts, and journalistic coverage. Taken together, these source materials are treated as institutionalized performances of a collectively held sociotechnical imaginary through which AGI is stabilized and reproduced. As such, AGI is positioned as the next supposedly inevitable threshold on the road to superintelligence, imbued with the promise to solve all problems (a techno-solutionist register), bring prosperity (techno-utopian), pose an existential threat to humanity (techno-apocalyptic), and become no less than god (techno-theological). These rhetorical registers together capture AGI as an ineluctable sociotechnical imaginary, as it is being spoken into existence.

items.title: Designing the Decision Supply Chain: A Framework for Human-AI Complementarity in Organizations
items.abstract: Organizations are rapidly expanding their capacity to generate and process information through data, analytics, and artificial intelligence (AI), yet greater intelligence does not necessarily translate into coordinated organizational action. As AI increasingly participates in organizational decision-making, a central managerial challenge is shifting from generating information to designing systems that transform distributed intelligence into effective decisions, coordinated action, and organizational learning. This chapter introduces Decision Supply Chain, defined as the interconnected organizational system through which signals are sensed, information is interpreted, alternatives are generated and evaluated, decisions are authorized, actions are executed, and outcomes inform subsequent decisions. The concept shifts the unit of analysis from individual decisions toward the architecture and coordination of interdependent decision activities across actors, technologies, and organizational boundaries. Although represented as a chain, the Decision Supply Chain is conceptualized as a networked and recursive system incorporating feedback, interdependence, and learning. Drawing on bounded rationality (Simon, 1957), tacit knowledge (Polanyi, 1966), Organizational Information Processing Theory (Galbraith, 1974), and research on human-AI collaboration, delegation, complementarity, and task allocation (Fügener et al., 2022, 2026; Puranam, 2021; Shrestha et al., 2019), the chapter develops a framework for Decision Supply Chain Design. It proposes that the allocation, coordination, and governance of human and AI decision activities should vary according to five characteristics of the decision context: uncertainty, consequence, reversibility, frequency, and interdependence. The framework further identifies risks arising from inappropriate human-AI configurations, including misaligned optimization, erosion of tacit knowledge, diminished human agency, and weakened organizational learning. The chapter argues that advantage from AI may depend not only on superior algorithms or information-processing capacity but increasingly on an organization's ability to orchestrate complementary human and AI capabilities across interconnected decision processes. Decision Supply Chain Design therefore offers a systems-level perspective for understanding how organizations can convert AI-enabled intelligence into coordinated action and sustained organizational learning.

items.title: Development and evaluation of eduvate CBT as an integrated artificial intelligence powered assessment ecosystem
items.abstract: The growth of digital assessment has intensified concerns about examination integrity, grading efficiency, fairness, and responsible artificial intelligence (AI). This study evaluates Eduvate CBT, an integrated role-based assessment ecosystem combining examination administration, AI-assisted proctoring, automated objective grading, reviewable violation evidence, and learning analytics. A four-week quantitative evaluation covered 250 undergraduate examination sessions across four computing courses, with usability data from 15 instructors and 5 administrators. At the session level, proctoring achieved 94.8% accuracy (95% CI 91.3–96.9), 94.6% precision, 96.6% recall, and an F1-score of 95.6%. Automated grading agreed with instructor consensus for 742 of 750 sampled responses (98.9%; 95% CI 97.9–99.5) and processed the cohort in under 10 s, compared with an estimated 23.1 h of manual grading. The aggregate System Usability Scale score was 87.4 (SD = 5.8; 95% CI 84.7–90.1). Analytics identified six low-performing items in algorithmic complexity, demonstrating how assessment evidence can prompt instructional review. The findings support the feasibility of the integrated workflow, although generalisability is limited by the single-institution design, absence of a competing-system control, and unavailable formal inter-rater reliability estimates.

items.title: Differences in perceived influences and educational support needs of generative AI among medical and nursing students across educational levels: a descriptive qualitative study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has been extensively integrated into nursing and medical education, significantly transforming the academic practices of students. Nonetheless, the varying impacts of GAI on core competency development across educational stages remain ambiguous, with limited empirical evidence on hierarchical educational support needs. This study aimed to investigate the effects of GAI utilization on critical thinking, research competence, and academic integrity among Chinese nursing and medical students at undergraduate, master's, and doctoral levels, and to identify their specific needs for targeted GAI educational support. Methods This descriptive qualitative study analyzed semi‑structured interviews with 44 students (16 undergraduate, 16 master's, 12 doctoral) from a western Chinese medical university using inductive content analysis, with TAM and AI Literacy frameworks informing discussion. Results GAI usage patterns varied by academic level: undergraduates for coursework, versus postgraduates for literature reviews, experimental design, and data analysis. The dual academic impact featured enhanced critical thinking and knowledge acquisition, counterbalanced by risks of over-reliance, marginal clinical skill efficacy, and cognitive offloading—with research competency gains largely confined to postgraduates. A pronounced demand for systemic support, including teacher guidance and institutional training, pervaded all levels. Conclusion GAI differentially affects nursing/medical students' progression, warranting stage-specific support. We propose a three-stage TAM-extension model (PEOU‑driven, PU‑driven, critical‑reflective) to capture developmental trajectories, offering empirical grounds for tiered AI literacy curricula.

items.title: Does generative-ai feedback in formative assessment improve higher-order thinking: motivational pathways in vocational safety education
items.abstract: Occupational health and safety (OHS) education in vocational high schools requires higher-order thinking skills (HOTS), yet formative assessment is often limited by delayed teacher feedback. This study examined whether generative AI-supported formative assessment using ChatGPT and Gemini improved HOTS and learning motivation compared with conventional teacher-led assessment, and explored the relationship between perceptions of AI-assisted assessment, motivation, and HOTS. A posttest-only nonequivalent control group quasi-experimental design involved 60 Grade X Machining Engineering students at SMK Negeri 1 Padang, divided into two intact classes of 30 students each. HOTS was measured using a 20-item reasoned multiple-choice test covering Bloom’s cognitive levels C4–C6, while motivation and perceptions of AI-assisted assessment were measured using validated questionnaires. Independent-samples t-tests were used for the primary analysis, followed by exploratory partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) in the experimental group. No significant differences were found between the AI-assisted and conventional assessment groups in HOTS scores (81.73 vs. 80.87, p = .417, d = 0.21) or motivation (54.03 vs. 54.83, p = .497, d = −0.18). Within the experimental group, perceptions of AI-assisted assessment were positively associated with motivation (β = 0.743, p < .001), and motivation was positively associated with HOTS (β = 0.476, p = .023). Although the indirect effect was statistically significant (β = 0.354, p = .042), its bias-corrected confidence interval included zero, making the mediation evidence inconclusive. These findings do not demonstrate that AI-assisted formative assessment improves HOTS or motivation beyond conventional teacher feedback. However, the observed motivational relationships warrant further investigation using larger samples, baseline measurements, and longer interventions.

items.title: Effects of Two Passive Back-Support Exoskeletons on Muscle Activity and Joint Kinematics During Simulated Crab Fishing Tasks
items.abstract: Low back injuries are common among commercial fishermen and have been linked to physically demanding tasks involved in fishing operations. Occupational back-support exoskeletons (BSEs) may help reduce low back physical demands, but their effectiveness in commercial fishing has not been well studied. This study evaluated the effects of two passive BSEs on muscle activity and joint kinematics in 20 male participants performing simulated crab sorting and pot handling tasks with and without two rigid BSEs. Results showed that both BSEs significantly reduced erector spinae muscle activity, with larger reductions during crab sorting than during pot handling. BSE use also led to some unintended changes in abdominal and leg muscle activity and joint kinematics, depending on the task and device used. These findings suggest that BSEs may help reduce low back demands during commercial crabbing, while highlighting the need to further evaluate potential side effects, especially during long-term use under real-world fishing conditions.

Despite the growing use of AI tools like ChatGPT, Google Translate, and Grammarly, there is limited research in Oman on learners' attitudes and the implications of AI for vocabulary instruction. The qualitative data revealed that EFL Omani students relied heavily on ChatGPT (49.7%) as the most widely used AI tool, followed by Google Translate (21.2%), Gemini AI (17.9%), Grammarly (6.6%). In addition, the trust in AI (frequency: 60), followed by cross-checking the meaning with other reliable resources (frequency: 67), learner autonomy (frequency: 67), and academic honesty (frequency: 64), but learning grammar, enhancing writing and reading skills had the lowest frequency. The quantitative data indicate an overall mean score of 3.67, suggesting a high frequency of AI tool use for vocabulary learning. The lowest mean score, 3.45, corresponds to the students' trust in the new vocabulary suggested by AI tools. In contrast, the effectiveness of AI tools received the highest mean score of 3.92. Additionally, it was found that AI tools, learners' attitudes and challenges, learning strategies, digital literacy, and how factors such as gender and academic level affect AI-assisted vocabulary learning in EFL Omani students were examined for vocabulary acquisition.

items.title: Enhancing ADAS Training: Examining the Effects of Training Modes and Styles on Driver Knowledge and Decision-Making
items.abstract: As Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) become increasingly common in modern vehicles, drivers often misunderstand how these systems work and when they reach their limits, which can lead to unsafe driving behaviors. This study examined how training modes (video vs. in-vehicle) and training styles (demonstration vs. practice) affect drivers’ ADAS knowledge improvement and decision-making accuracy when responding to system limitations. Sixty participants were assigned to one of four conditions covering three Level 1 and Level 2 ADAS features: Adaptive Cruise Control, Lane Keeping Assist, and Partial Automation. In-vehicle training produced greater knowledge gains than video-based training overall. For Partial Automation specifically, in-vehicle demonstration and video-based practice both outperformed video demonstration. However, knowledge improvement did not translate to better decision-making accuracy in any condition. These findings suggest that ADAS training should go beyond teaching system limitations and also help drivers apply that knowledge when system limitations occur during driving.

items.title: Entrepreneurship Education for Inclusive AI and Sustainable Growth: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming entrepreneurship by enhancing innovation, decision-making, and operational efficiency. However, unequal access to technology, limited digital literacy, and ethical concerns constrain inclusive AI adoption, particularly among underserved entrepreneurial communities. This study systematically reviews how entrepreneurship education promotes inclusive AI adoption and supports sustainable business growth. Guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, the study examined literature published between 2015 and 2025 across five databases: Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, and SpringerLink. Following screening and eligibility assessment, 54 studies were included. Findings indicate that AI literacy, adaptive learning platforms, digital mentorship, and practical business simulations can strengthen entrepreneurial competencies, innovation, and data-driven decision-making. Inclusive AI adoption is also associated with improved operational efficiency, competitiveness, and resource utilization. However, barriers include inadequate digital infrastructure, high implementation costs, algorithmic bias, and data privacy concerns. The review highlights limited evidence on long-term outcomes and environmental sustainability. Drawing on Human Capital Theory, the Technology Acceptance Model, and Innovation Diffusion Theory, the study contributes an integrated perspective on inclusive AI, entrepreneurship education, and sustainability. It recommends inclusive curricula, ethical AI governance, accessible infrastructure, and targeted policy support to promote equitable and sustainable entrepreneurial growth.

items.title: Ethics of artificial intelligence use in dermatology research and healthcare
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming dermatology at a rapid pace unlike any other clinical specialty, largely because skin disease is diagnosed visually and, therefore, lends itself naturally to image-based machine learning. Convolutional neural networks now correspond with dermatologists in classifying pigmented lesions, teledermatology platforms triage patients across vast distances, and AI-enabled applications are increasingly available on patients’ screens. Yet this rapid uptake has outpaced the ethical and regulatory scaffolding needed to govern it safely. The Indian Council of Medical Research has addressed this gap conscientiously in March 2023 by publishing the Ethical Guidelines for Application of AI in Biomedical Research and Healthcare, India’s first dedicated ethics framework for medical AI. This article examines the ethical dimensions of AI in dermatology research and clinical practice through the lens of these guidelines, drawing on dermatology-specific evidence on algorithmic bias, consent, data privacy, transparency, and accountability, with recommendations for dermatologists, researchers, and ethics committees engaging with this technology.

items.title: Exploring generative AI appropriation in Colombian adults’ informal English learning
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming the possibilities for informal language learning by providing immediate feedback, conversational interaction, and potentially personalized learning experiences. However, its use does not necessarily entail greater learner autonomy, self-regulation, or agency. This study aimed to understand how Colombian adults configure their informal English learning practices through GenAI tools, with particular attention to decision-making processes, self-regulation, evaluation of AI-generated responses, and the articulation of GenAI with other learning resources. Adopting a qualitative, exploratory, and interpretive approach, the study involved four Colombian adults with diverse linguistic, educational, and GenAI-use trajectories. Data were generated through participant characterization forms, GenAI interaction records, semi-structured interviews, and, when available, documentary evidence of participants’ interactions with the technology. A predominantly inductive thematic analysis generated four interconnected categories: negotiating control over the learning interaction; constructing and calibrating trust in AI-generated feedback; experiencing personalization through responsive interaction; and reconfiguring the broader learning repertoire. Findings show that participants assumed, negotiated, and delegated control in different ways and developed varying criteria for accepting, questioning, or verifying GenAI-generated responses. They also selectively integrated GenAI with other digital and human learning resources. Based on these findings, the study conceptualizes GenAI appropriation as a form of situated orchestration through which learners coordinate technological affordances with their purposes, prior knowledge, evaluative criteria, and broader learning repertoires. The findings suggest that GenAI does not automatically produce learner autonomy or agency; rather, it creates new spaces in which these may be exercised, negotiated, or delegated.

items.title: Familiar Style and Calibrated Correction in Repeated AI Use. A framework for style recognition discrimination and substantive correction
items.abstract: Repeated users of an artificial-intelligence agent may learn both its competence and how it sounds. This paper proposes that acquired style congruence can change acceptance independently of evidential quality, while any benefit to error management may arise through more than one route. Learned style–correctness contingencies can guide classification; reduced processing demands may also free attention for substantive checking when style itself is non-diagnostic. The framework distinguishes recognition, response criterion, classification sensitivity, competence learning, defect identification, successful correction, and final accuracy. Five competing mechanisms are specified: familiarity halo, anomaly vigilance, diagnostic cue learning, competence learning, and processing-efficiency learning. Building on appropriate-reliance research, calibration symmetry is treated as a requirement for identification and measurement: both familiar-looking wrong answers and unfamiliar-looking correct answers must be examined. It does not imply equal frequency, cost, or normative importance. The contribution is a bounded synthesis for acquired, source-specific style, not a new general principle of reliance or a demonstrated familiarity effect. Study 1 crosses acquired style congruence with correctness while preserving randomized assignment and measuring inferred source or version change. Study 2 varies cue diagnosticity and distinguishes classification through style from identifying and repairing substantive defects. Outcome feedback, trial-level learning, delayed unaided performance, and transfer are specified separately from assisted performance. Conversational affirmation and linguistic accommodation are adjacent pathways, not evidence of acquired-style effects. Governance implications remain provisional pending direct evidence.

items.title: Fault Tolerance in IoT Networks for Industrial Automation Using Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) has become a fundamental component of modern industrial automation by connecting sensors, actuators, programmable logic controllers, robotic systems, machines, edge devices, and cloud platforms for continuous monitoring and intelligent control. However, the dependence of industrial operations on interconnected IoT networks introduces significant risks associated with communication failures, sensor faults, hardware degradation, software errors, cyber-attacks, congestion, and edge computing failures. A single failure can interrupt production, reduce product quality, increase maintenance costs, or create safety hazards. This paper examines the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve fault tolerance in IoT networks used for industrial automation. The paper reviews recent developments in AI based fault detection, anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, intelligent routing, and edge based recovery, and adaptive resource management. Recent studies demonstrate that machine learning can identify abnormal device and sensor behavior before failures propagate, while Software Defined Networking can support rapid route restoration and network recovery. AI enabled edge computing further reduces response latency by moving fault analysis closer to industrial devices. The paper proposes a conceptual AI enabled fault tolerant architecture consisting of an IoT sensing layer, resilient communication layer, edge intelligence layer, AI fault analysis layer, decision and recovery layer, and industrial control layer. The proposed approach combines real-time monitoring, machine-learning-based prediction, redundant communication paths, automated recovery, and predictive maintenance. The paper concludes that integrating AI with fault-tolerance mechanisms can improve industrial network availability, reliability, resilience, and operational continuity. Nevertheless, challenges involving data quality, explain ability, computational resources, cyber security, interoperability, and validation in real industrial environments require further investigation.

items.title: From appropriate use to dependency: How AI attitude and use motivations shape university students’ AI dependency
items.abstract: Abstract Whether students develop dependence on generative artificial intelligence (AI) technologies largely depends on their attitudes toward using such tools. Existing studies have primarily explained the formation of AI dependence from the perspectives of usage attitudes and technological characteristics, while paying limited attention to the psychological mechanisms through which attitudes exert their influence. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory, the present study examines how different types of use motivation mediate the relationship between students’ AI attitudes and AI dependence. A total of 405 university students completed a comprehensive questionnaire measuring AI attitudes, use motivations, and AI dependence. The results indicate that: (i) AI attitudes do not directly predict AI dependence; instead, their effects are transmitted through multiple motivational pathways, with intrinsic motivation inhibiting AI dependence, whereas identified regulation facilitates its development; (ii) three distinct AI dependence profiles were identified: dependent, moderate, and conservative users. These profiles exhibited clear stratification, with dependent users showing the highest scores across all dimensions and conservative users the lowest; and (iii) individuals with stronger motivations are more likely to be classified into the dependent user profile, with external motivation playing a particularly salient role. These findings enrich the literature on AI technology dependence and offer practical implications for higher education administrators, tool developers, and educational researchers.

items.title: From Operational Disruption to Intelligent Service Operations: A Practitioner Journey with Autonomous AI Agents
items.abstract: The COVID-19 disruption and subsequent talent mobility exposed important vulnerabilities in traditional service operations. Organizations relying heavily on individual expertise faced risks to operational continuity when experienced professionals moved roles or left. Although knowledge transfer, standard operating procedures, and documentation remain essential, they do not always capture the contextual knowledge developed through years of resolving incidents. The resulting gaps can affect service quality, turnaround time, operating costs, and user experience. This chapter examines how human-AI collaboration can strengthen operational resilience and knowledge continuity in service operations. It draws on the practitioner journey behind IgnitronX.AI, a cloud-native multi-agent platform developed to address enterprise operational challenges using generative AI and agentic AI. Its architecture supports service teams by surfacing similar historical incidents, recommending potential resolutions, enabling knowledge discovery, summarizing operational records, and providing sentiment insights. The objective is not to replace human expertise but to augment it. The implementation journey demonstrated that technology alone cannot deliver sustainable value. Data quality emerged as a critical constraint, alongside security, confidentiality, framework and model selection, operating-cost management, governance, and stakeholder adoption. The experience also reinforced that organizations should first understand the business problem, simplify processes, remove waste, and make deliberate build-versus-buy decisions. Through this reflective practitioner case, the chapter offers leaders practical insights into intelligent operations that preserve organizational knowledge, strengthen service continuity, and create the potential for improved productivity, operational efficiency, and user experience through responsible human-AI collaboration.

items.title: Generative AI in Higher Education: Adoption, Risks, and Opportunities in the Nordic Region
items.abstract: This study investigates how students and academic staff in Nordic higher education engage with generative artificial intelligence. It asks what drives students to continue using these tools after initial adoption, and how academic staff perceive the opportunities and risks they bring. The study is grounded in the Technology Continuance Theory, which holds that continued use is shaped by perceived usefulness, satisfaction, and confirmation, with trust and perceived security added as contextual factors relevant to the Nordic setting.The research was conducted across five Nordic countries: Sweden, Finland, Norway, Denmark, and Iceland. A mixed-methods sequential design was used. The quantitative phase involved an online questionnaire administered to higher education students across the region, analysed using Generalized Structured Component Analysis to test the hypothesised relationships between the constructs. The qualitative phase involved semi-structured interviews with professors, analysed thematically to capture the perspectives of academic staff on the use of generative AI in teaching and learning, with particular attention to linguistic representation and institutional practice. The two phases were integrated to provide a fuller picture of adoption than either method could offer alone.

items.title: GENERATIVE AI IN MODERN EDUCATION: ETHICAL IMPLICATIONS AND ACADEMIC INTEGRITY
items.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence has significantly transformed contemporary education by introducing new opportunities for teaching, learning, assessment, and academic research. AI-powered systems can generate written texts, explain complex concepts, provide personalised feedback, and support independent learning. However, their increasing use has raised important ethical concerns regarding academic integrity, plagiarism, authorship, data privacy, algorithmic bias, and the reliability of AI-generated information. This article examines the role of generative AI in modern educational environments, focusing on its pedagogical benefits, ethical implications, and influence on academic standards. It explores the responsibilities of students, teachers, researchers, and educational institutions in promoting the transparent and responsible use of AI technologies. The article argues that generative AI should be integrated into education through clear institutional policies, effective digital literacy programmes, and assessment methods that emphasise critical thinking, creativity, and independent understanding. Responsible AI integration can support educational innovation while preserving the fundamental principles of academic integrity and intellectual responsibility.

items.title: Generative AI-supported peace pedagogy in higher education: A two-wave quasi-experimental study of AI literacy, intercultural sensitivity, and empathy
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used in higher education, but its value for humanistic learning depends on pedagogical designs that preserve learner judgment and require critical evaluation of generated content. This two-wave quasi-experimental study examined a six-week GenAI-supported peace-pedagogy module in 522 Saudi higher-education students (intervention n = 276; waitlist n = 246). Intercultural sensitivity, empathy, and AI literacy were assessed at pretest and posttest using the ISS-15, Interpersonal Reactivity Index, and an adapted Arabic administration of the Meta AI Literacy Scale (MAILS), respectively. Primary analyses used linear mixed-effects models for Time × Group interactions, with baseline-adjusted posttest ANCOVA models as sensitivity analyses; network analyses were secondary and exploratory. The groups differed at baseline on all three primary outcomes. The intervention group showed a larger increase in intercultural sensitivity (interaction b = 0.699, 95% CI [0.524, 0.875], BH-adjusted p < .001), and the baseline-adjusted posttest difference remained substantial (b = 1.042, 95% CI [0.918, 1.165], BH-adjusted p < .001). AI literacy showed a similar, smaller pattern (interaction b = 0.333, 95% CI [0.148, 0.517], BH-adjusted p < .001; baseline-adjusted posttest b = 0.639, 95% CI [0.534, 0.744], BH-adjusted p < .001). Empathy did not show robust evidence of improvement: the Time × Group interaction was negative (b = −0.252, 95% CI [−0.409, −0.095], p = .002), whereas the baseline-adjusted posttest group difference was not significant (b = 0.034, 95% CI [−0.083, 0.151], p = .572). Exploratory network comparisons did not detect significant group differences at either wave. Overall, the intervention group showed larger gains in self-reported intercultural sensitivity and AI literacy, whereas empathy showed no robust positive pattern. Because allocation was nonrandom, groups differed at baseline, attrition could not be reconstructed, and the comparison group received usual coursework, the findings cannot establish a causal effect or isolate GenAI’s contribution.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Governance and Algorithmic Trust in Smart Organizations: Implications for Sustainable Innovation and Organizational Performance
items.abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being integrated into knowledge work, organizational decision support, and sustainability-related operations, yet evidence regarding governance, algorithmic trust, and durable organizational value remains fragmented. This article develops an integrated explanation of how responsible governance can enable, rather than merely constrain, the creation of sustainable innovation and organizational performance. Design/methodology/approach A critical, structured integrative synthesis draws on recent peer-reviewed research and authoritative policy and standards publications issued between 2023 and October 2026. Sources compared through thematic coding across governance architecture, calibrated algorithmic trust, human-AI collaboration, sustainable innovation, and organizational performance. The article proposes constructs, testable propositions, an implementation framework, and a future empirical research design; it does not claim to report original survey or experimental findings. Findings Governance quality theorized to improve organizational outcomes through calibrated trust and responsible human-AI practices. The effects are contingent on decision criticality, employee AI literacy, accountability arrangements, institutional pressure, and the environmental costs of computation. Trust appropriately calibrated to system reliability rather than maximized. Practical implications Organizations should combine documented use-case inventories, risk-tiered oversight, evaluation, traceability, worker participation, and multidimensional scorecards. Originality/value the framework connects governance mechanisms and behavioral trust calibration to an explicitly triple-bottom-line account of innovation and performance, while separating established empirical evidence from propositions requiring testing.

items.abstract: Hallucination Is All You Need: When AI Dreams Meet the Hospitality Labor Crisis Po-Chen Chen THE AMNIS, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Kaohsiung, Taiwan Email:amnischenadrian@gmail.com ——————————————————————————————————————— Abstract This paper examines the relationship between anthropomorphic narratives in artificial intelligence (AI), the technical capabilities of contemporary computational systems, and the material labor challenges facing the hospitality industry. Through a fourfold conceptual analysis, the paper investigates how metaphorical representations of AI may influence public understanding of technological capabilities and expectations regarding the automation of physical service work. First, it distinguishes the mathematical and statistical mechanisms underlying large language models from interpretations that attribute human-like subjective experience to their outputs. Second, it examines Dream-RSI as a case study in the use of biological metaphors to describe computational processes, distinguishing replay-based exploration-policy improvement from human dreaming or subconscious reflection. Third, it considers the physical and engineering constraints of AI infrastructure and discusses their implications for the deployment of robotic systems in hospitality environments. Fourth, it explores how narratives of technological transformation may influence investment expectations and operational decision-making in labor-intensive industries. The paper argues that technological capabilities should be evaluated according to demonstrated performance rather than anthropomorphic expectations. It further identifies targeted mechanical automation, workforce development, and responsible international labor mobility as potential approaches to addressing hospitality labor shortages, while recognizing the need for context-specific economic and empirical evaluation. By connecting AI narratives with the material requirements of service delivery, this paper proposes a framework for examining the relationship between technological expectation, operational feasibility, and the future of human labor in hospitality. Keywords: AI Anthropomorphism; Hallucination; Dream-RSI; Hospitality Labor Crisis; Humanoid Robots; Migrant Workers; Capital Allocation.

items.title: Healthy crew, healthy life: The captain’s role in commercial fishing crew health
items.abstract: Objectives Commercial fishermen engage in one of the most dangerous professions in the United States. This qualitative study explored how the internal priorities of commercial fishermen captains influence the health and well-being of their crew members. Methods Data were collected via semi-structured qualitative interviews conducted under the 2025 Southeast and Gulf Coast Fishing First Aid and Safety Training program. Commercial fishermen and individuals working adjacent to the industry (n = 10) were recruited using purposive sampling. Using a priori qualitative coding, two coders performed a thematic analysis using ATLAS.ti. Results Overall, participants reported that crew health and wellness were affected by the captain’s attitudes. Participants (40%) explored crew preparedness as a central theme in captains’ approaches to crew well-being, with the captain’s knowledge of pre-existing conditions allowing for a proactive approach to medication management and injury/illness reduction (30%). Some (20%) highlighted a conflict of priorities between crew productivity and well-being or observed that captains’ attitudes towards zero-tolerance policy against substance use would influence substance use onboard the vessel (20%). Conclusion Preparing captains and crew members with safety knowledge and skills can mitigate predictable hazards. These findings highlight the importance of continued research and programming surrounding proactive health management among commercial fishermen captains.

items.title: Heart rate variability as a physiological marker of motion sickness in real-world driving conditions
items.abstract: This study investigated the utility of heart rate variability (HRV) metrics derived from electrocardiogram (ECG) signals for assessing motion sickness (MS) during real-world driving. While motion sickness is commonly evaluated through subjective reports or multimodal physiological measurements, previous studies have predominantly relied on simulator-based experiments or multimodal physiological sensing, which limit ecological validity and practical deployment in everyday vehicles. In this study, twenty-four female participants were exposed to systematically varied acceleration and deceleration profiles across 13 predefined driving conditions in an electric vehicle. Motion sickness symptoms were measured using the Misery Scale (MISC), and ECG data were segmented into 120-s epochs to extract heart rate, the low-frequency to high-frequency (LF/HF) ratio, and pNN50 (the percentage of successive normal-to-normal intervals differing by more than 50 ms). Using a threshold corresponding to symptom onset (MISC of 2 or above), pNN50 was significantly lower in the high-MS group than in the low-MS group (16.5% versus 24.6%, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = -0.53), indicating reduced parasympathetic (vagal) modulation in the presence of motion sickness symptoms. Heart rate did not differ significantly between groups, and the LF/HF ratio showed a statistically significant but negligible difference. Mean pNN50 values did not, however, decline monotonically across individual MISC scores, indicating that the metric distinguishes the presence of symptoms rather than grading their severity. These findings suggest that pNN50 is the most sensitive of the examined HRV indices and may reflect individual differences in susceptibility to motion sickness. The study demonstrates that motion sickness can be assessed using a single, widely accessible physiological signal such as ECG, providing a foundation for future wearable and in-vehicle motion sickness monitoring systems.

items.title: HOW TO FIND AND ENJOY CREATIVITY : On Attentive Observation, the Hedgehog Concept, and Why Guessing Is Not Creating
items.abstract: The current AI industry claims that large language models are creative. They generate text, images, music, code. They produce novelty. They are called creative. This paper argues that generation is not creativity. The paper makes three claims: First: Creativity is the selection of what matters. Selection requires a criterion. The criterion is the Hedgehog Concept — the intersection of what you are deeply passionate about, what you can be the best in the world at, and what drives your economic engine. It is discovered through attentive observation. Second: An LLM generates by guessing. It samples from a distribution over an unbounded space. It has no criterion. It cannot select. It is not creative. Third: The human who has discovered their Hedgehog Concept is creative by breathing.Once the criterion is found, creativity is the result of attentive observation. It is not effort. It is the natural state of a person who has found what they were sent here to do. The paper is written for the reader who wants to find their creativity and enjoy it. It is not a manual. It is a record of how the discovery works.

items.title: How Will We Know Second-Generation AI? (AI's Green Tomatoes)
items.abstract: An essay from The Bush Book. Today’s AI models are picked green: grown in the lab, polished to please raters like tomatoes gassed to look ripe, then frozen and shipped. What users then correct and teach them in live work ripens only on their own “windowsills” or dissolves in one big common pot. The essay proposes the missing stage — a “residency” for models that are not yet frozen: selected specialists and attentive users act as mentors, their verified lessons are fed back into training, and their work is credited and paid or rewarded with perks. Power is one precondition, ripening on the vine is the second; but second-generation AI can be recognized only by its practical result — far fewer errors passing from drafts into the documents people act on (“First, do no harm”), measured by the hybrid survivability criterion. items.title: INSTRUCTIONAL DESIGN OF A WORKPLACE-ORIENTED GENERAL AIGC COURSE IN THE ERA OF DIGITAL INTELLIGENCE
items.abstract: In the era of digital intelligence, artificial intelligence generated content (AIGC) has become deeply integrated into workplace workflows. However, a growing gap has emerged between corporate demand for AIGC-driven productivity and the lag in talent development. Current introductory AIGC courses suffer from fragmented content, superficial assessment methods, and limited adaptability. To address these challenges, this study proposes a holistic instructional design framework based on the "structural reconstruction, capability building, and closed-loop evaluation" model, featuring an 8-hour modular curriculum: prompt engineering (2 hours) to establish foundational concepts for cross-domain transfer, core tool mastery (4 hours) covering four mainstream AI platforms (ERNIE Bot, DeepSeek, WPS AI, and Doubao), and role-specific applications (2 hours) offering tailored practical exercises across five key professions (finance, education, software development, copywriting, and design). The framework employs a hybrid assessment model combining self-evaluations, instructor feedback, and AI-driven evaluations to target real-world problem-solving skills and adaptability to new tools, while a data-driven feedback loop enables continuous optimization of both course content and personalized learning interventions. Ultimately, this study provides a scalable, iterative system framework for empowering today's AI-driven workforce.

items.title: Integration of AI in Education Toward Future-Ready Assessments
items.abstract: This research examines the dual impact of artificial intelligence in education, in response to the rapid development of AI technologies. The study explores how AI can enhance learning efficiency and educational outcomes while presenting challenges to academic integrity and fundamental skills development. Employing a mixed-methods approach, the study involved 44 EFL students in Oman and surveyed 102 students from various educational institutions. Researchers analyzed students’ performance in both AI-assisted and traditional writing tasks while observing behavioral patterns and attitudes toward these technologies. Key findings revealed a 42% reduction in grammatical errors with AI assistance, yet 63% of students failed to fully follow instructions, demonstrating limited deep content understanding. While 91% of students reported using AI tools, 60.4% expressed the need for training in ethical usage. The study concludes with three critical recommendations: developing clear institutional policies for AI governance, redesigning assessment methods to focus on learning processes rather than products and strengthening academic values and transparency. These proposals align with the vision of balancing innovation with adaptation to technological change.

items.title: Integration of Auditory and Tactile Information in Time-to-Contact Estimation
items.abstract: This study investigated the integration of auditory and tactile information in time-to-contact (TTC) estimation for objects moving with constant velocity (Experiment 1) and constant acceleration (Experiment 2). Participants estimated TTC using a prediction-motion task under auditory, tactile, and audio-tactile conditions to determine whether people can use vibrotactile stimuli to judge TTC and whether concurrent cues improve judgments compared to single modalities. Analyses of absolute constant error revealed a sensory modality effect in Experiment 2, where audio-tactile stimuli produced lower error than tactile alone, but not in Experiment 1. Variable error showed greater audio-tactile precision over tactile-only stimuli across both experiments, though audio-tactile performance never differed from auditory-only cues. These findings are consistent with the revised tau theory, in which people combine first-order information from several sources to make TTC estimations.

items.title: Inteligência artificial na educação e neuroplasticidade: contribuições, limites e desafios para a aprendizagem
items.abstract: The literature on artificial intelligence (AI) in education focuses almost exclusively on performance, perception, and engagement; brain changes associated with neuroplasticity have rarely been measured. This narrative review, using explicit search and classification criteria, distinguishes three types of evidence: (a) learning outcomes (grades, retention, and transfer), (b) behavioral measures of cognitive effort, and (c) direct neurophysiological measures (EEG and fNIRS). The most robust performance studies indicate that the effects of AI depend on task design: a randomized trial involving approximately one thousand high school students found gains ranging from 48% to 127% during AI-assisted practice, while performance declined on an exam taken without AI among students with unrestricted access to the model; this decline was eliminated when the system was configured to provide hints rather than answers. The most frequently cited meta-analysis supporting AI (g = 0.867) was retracted in 2026 due to analytical errors and the inclusion of invalid studies. The few studies using brain-based measures are small (n ranging from 24 to 54), short in duration, unpublished in peer-reviewed journals or reporting null findings, and assess momentary engagement rather than lasting structural or functional plasticity. It is therefore concluded that there is no basis for claiming that AI, by itself, either enhances or impairs neuroplasticity. The evidence supports a narrower conclusion: activities that replace retrieval and elaborative effort tend to reduce measured learning, whereas activities that preserve such effort tend to maintain or enhance learning gains. A research agenda is proposed incorporating longitudinal designs, transfer measures, and pre- and post-intervention neuroimaging with active control conditions.

items.title: Intelligent Academic Software: Transforming Higher Education through AI-Driven Learning Ecosystems
items.abstract: The digital transformation of higher education has accelerated with the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies into academic software systems. Intelligent Academic Software (IAS) represents a paradigm shift from static learning management systems toward dynamic, data-driven learning ecosystems capable of personalization, predictive analytics, automated assessment, and institutional decision support. This study proposes a comprehensive AI-driven learning ecosystem model integrating adaptive learning engines, intelligent tutoring systems, predictive analytics modules, and administrative automation frameworks. A multi-institutional dataset comprising 1,200 student records was analyzed using supervised and unsupervised machine learning algorithms to evaluate performance prediction, engagement analytics, and risk detection accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate improved academic performance forecasting (92% accuracy), enhanced learner engagement, and optimized resource allocation. The study contributes to AI-enabled higher education transformation by presenting a scalable intelligent software architecture aligned with ethical AI governance and institutional digital strategies.

items.title: Investigating the Impact of AI-Facilitated Socratic Dialogue on Critical Thinking Skills
items.abstract: This mixed-method study aims to explore the impact of having Socratic dialogue with artificial intelligence (AI) on students' critical thinking skills’ performance. The data were gathered from 35 foundation-level students. The study utilised a Watson Glaser critical thinking pre-test and post-test to measure their critical thinking abilities and a questionnaire to gather their perception of AI usage. During the intervention, students were engaged in structured AI-facilitated Socratic questioning sessions weekly. Data were analysed using paired-sample t-tests and linear regression, while survey responses were examined for thematic trends. Even though the data collected shows that students have a positive perception of using AI, there is no statistically significant difference between the pre- and post-tests (p > .05). The finding shows that students’ critical thinking performance did not improve throughout the study. Furthermore, the results for the linear regression (R² = 0.038, p > .05) show that there is very little correlation between students’ perception and their critical thinking performance. The study reveals the gap between students’ positive perception of using AI and their critical thinking skill development.

items.title: Leveraging Mental Models for Human-Centered Explanations: A Systematic Design Approach Illustrated by Explainable Fake Review Identification
items.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) often prioritizes model fidelity over user intelligibility, yielding explanations that satisfy technical transparency yet fail to support human sense-making. We propose a human-centered approach, MIND-X (Mental-model INtegrated Design for eXplainability), which aligns explanations with users' mental models, commonsense concepts, and judgment heuristics. Using fake review detection as a case study, we contribute: (1) a qualitative study (n=10) that elicits how people assess review credibility and produces an actionable, design-guiding taxonomy of perceptual cues; (2) a set of design principles that link those cues to explanation strategies and prompt LLMs to generate adaptive, language-based explanations; and (3) a quantitative evaluation (n=166) showing that these explanations offer distinct advantages over token-level transparency methods widely used in explainable text classification in terms of understandability, satisfaction, perceived trust, persuasiveness, and decision-making support. Rather than claiming general superiority, our evaluation illustrates how grounding explanations in users' everyday reasoning practices can produce more intelligible and context-sensitive accounts. Our findings advance human-centered explanation design beyond a mere "gloss of transparency," demonstrating that a mental-model-aligned design process can improve intelligibility and support accountability across user-centered explanation tasks.

items.title: Localizing AI in Rural India: The Role of Talent Management in Reconfiguring Agricultural Knowledge Systems
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into agriculture-focused development agendas, its use in rural field settings challenges current thinking about fit, equity, and sustainability. This paper examines the overlooked dimensions of how talent management processes impact the sociotechnical localization of AI in rural agricultural ecosystems in India. Based on multi-sited qualitative case studies in Karnataka, Bihar, and Maharashtra, we explore how talent pipelines, including agri-digital intermediaries, AI translators, and local facilitators, mediate the adoption, translation, and incorporation of AI tools by small institutional and professional farmers. The findings suggest that human infrastructure is not merely supportive but constitutive of the successful integration of AI, especially in settings characterized by educational asymmetries, caste hierarchies, and gendered exclusions. Informed by sociotechnical systems theory and the concepts of knowledge coproduction and epistemic justice, this research contends that talent management must be reimagined as a fundamental infrastructural and ethical spine for digital innovation. The analysis conceptualizes AI localization as a negotiated alignment between algorithmic systems and agrarian lifeworlds made possible by contextually embedded, culturally literate, and institutionally embedded human agents. This helps push the boundaries of what it means for AI to be technically feasible, socially situated, and democratically transformed in the Global South.

items.title: Marketing to Machines: Strategic Frameworks for Engagement with Autonomous Agentic AI
items.abstract: The evolution of Generative AI from passive recommendation engines into autonomous Agentic AI is fundamentally redefining the landscape of consumer decision-making and value creation. As consumers increasingly delegate choice evaluation, dynamic negotiation, and purchasing execution to software agents, traditional marketing paradigms centered on human psychological persuasion are losing their strategic effectiveness. This chapter critically examines the emerging dynamics of "Marketing to Machines" (M2M), proposing a comprehensive conceptual model, the Algorithm-to-Algorithm (A2A) Engagement Framework, to illustrate how modern enterprises can strategically align their market offerings with autonomous machine buyers. To build this framework, we conduct an integrative synthesis of peer-reviewed literature published between 2015 and 2026 across marketing strategy, information systems, computer science, and behavioral economics, selected through systematic topic-based sampling. The synthesis reaches key theoretical and practical conclusions across four structural dimensions: the transition from emotional branding to structured data and metadata optimization (Generative Engine Optimization), the mechanics of real-time machine-to-machine value negotiation, the restructuring of traditional brand equity into algorithmic trust, and the ethical alignment of enterprise offerings with automated choice architectures through transparent governance and data integrity. The chapter embeds an explicit ethical framework to evaluate algorithmic neutrality, fairness, and consumer regulatory compliance. To demonstrate real-world applicability, the conceptual model is grounded in an analytical examination of established commercial autonomous agent environments and digital governance protocols. Ultimately, the conclusions of this chapter indicate that long-term competitive advantage in an agent-dominated market relies heavily on data machine-readability, operational transparency, API-driven fulfillment, and ethical algorithmic reputation management, providing actionable guidance for re-engineering Go-To-Market strategies when the primary buyer is an autonomous algorithm.

items.title: Methodology for the application of generative artificial intelligence tools in higher design education
items.abstract: The rapid development of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) technologies across both theoretical and practical domains is fundamentally transforming the epistemological and pedagogical foundations of higher design education. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the methodological integration of generative AI tools, including ChatGPT, Claude, Midjourney, and DALL·E, in fostering creative thinking, critical analysis, and practical skills among design students in higher education institutions. The research examines the transition of studio pedagogy from traditional forms toward hybrid and dialogical models, the reinterpretation of Donald Schön’s concept of reflection-in-action within algorithmic environments, and the evolving role of the educator in AI-assisted learning processes. Methodologically, the study is grounded in a modified Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework and a four-component Information and Communication Competence (ICC) model. The findings indicate that the systematic and purposeful implementation of GAI tools can increase students’ visual design production and productivity by approximately 14%; however, it may also lead to reduced diversity of ideas and an overreliance on algorithms for cognitive functions. To mitigate these risks, the study proposes the concepts of epistemic vigilance and process-oriented hybrid assessment mechanisms as essential components of contemporary design education.

items.title: Miasma: an open-source, lightweight countermeasure against unauthorized AI web scraping
items.abstract: The widespread adoption of large language models has greatly increased demand for publicly accessible web data, resulting in increased web scraping across the internet. The resulting bandwidth and compute costs fall on site operators rather than on the parties collecting the data, with scientific databases and journals among those reporting service disruption [1]. Existing mitigations such as rate limiting, CAPTCHAs, and robots.txt rules can discourage well-behaved crawlers, but impose no cost on scrapers that choose to ignore them. Deception-based alternatives have shown promise, though prominent examples such as Cloudflare’s AI Labyrinth remain tied to enterprise platforms [2]. Separately, recent work suggests that small quantities of poisoned content can compromise a model [3], and that continual training on low-quality content measurably degrades model performance [4]. Miasma is an open-source tarpit that brings a deception-based defense within reach of small operators. Implemented in Rust, it runs as a standalone service or as an embeddable library, trapping unwanted crawlers in a recursively generated network of links whose pages carry deliberately poisoned content. Miasma does not perform bot detection itself. Rather, it is paired with an upstream mechanism such as hidden links or an existing detection tool, and its poisoned content is drawn from a configurable external source. Instead of blocking requests outright, Miasma reduces the value of what is collected while keeping its own operational footprint small. To that end, Miasma uses asynchronous request handling on the tokio runtime, a bounded in-flight request cap that places a hard limit on memory consumption, and a custom HTML templating system that streams page chunks without allocating intermediate strings. Miasma is able to serve 100 sustained in-flight requests while using roughly 50 MB of memory. Across six months of deployment on a small portfolio site, Miasma served 210 million requests and 1.29 TB of poisoned content. As of October 2026, the project has reached 1,200+ stars and 6 contributors on GitHub, with 6,500+ Docker pulls, and is distributed under GPL-3.0 via Cargo, Docker, and community-maintained packages.

items.title: Modeling the Coevolution of Human Skills and AI Adoption
items.abstract: The value of relying on generative AI depends on two quantities that evolve with its use: users' unaided skill, which may decline without practice, and the originality of AI-assisted work, which may decline as more people rely on similar tools. We model this process as a coevolutionary game in which individuals choose between autonomous and AI-assisted work, with autonomous practice strengthening their skills while reliance on AI gradually erodes them. When the reinforcing effect of skill erosion outweighs the crowding cost of lost originality, the population exhibits two alternative stable states: low AI adoption with high average skill, and high AI adoption with low average skill. Because skill is individual, autonomous workers remain more skilled than AI users, making autonomous work less vulnerable to population-wide skill decline. The strength of this effect is governed by a timescale ratio: the rate at which skills adapt relative to the rate at which individuals change strategy. The same ratio determines the full distribution of skills, which we derive analytically. Populations with identical AI adoption and average skill can differ sharply: when strategies change frequently, skills remain homogeneous and collective lock-in to high AI adoption is stronger; when strategies persist, lock-in weakens but the population can polarize into highly skilled autonomous workers and AI-dependent individuals. Modeling output overlap further shows that more diverse AI outputs can make widespread adoption harder to reverse. Together, these results expose tradeoffs between the benefits of widespread AI adoption and its long-run risks, making collective lock-in and skill polarization distinct intervention targets.

Finally, Age has a significant and negative relationship with AIJRA (β = − 0.121, P ≤ 0.05).Conclusion: The Study’s findings underscore the importance of individual factors such as AISE in enhancing the role of POS on AILA. items.abstract: Module Description This module combines open pedagogy, renewable assignments, reflective practice, AI literacy, collaborative learning, student-generated knowledge, peer review, open licensing, and repository-based dissemination, based on the Repositories of AI Literacy Resources (RAILR) concept. The module is primarily designed for undergraduate students, although it can be adapted for other educational levels depending on the instructor's teaching goals. It can be delivered as a standalone module, an elective, or with its learning activities incorporated into an existing course. The central purpose of the module is to move students beyond being consumers of AI literacy guidance resources to becoming creators. Through reflection on their own experiences of using generative AI tools, discussion with peers, collaborative resource development, peer review, and open dissemination, students can develop AI literacy resources that can benefit other learners. Instructors are not required to treat every activity as compulsory, except when implementing the module as a full course or an elective. Instead, instructors can select and adapt the activities according to their course objectives, teaching goals, available teaching time, student numbers, and preferred or feasible mode of delivery. Learning Outcomes By the end of this module, students should be able to: Explain the concept of open pedagogy and distinguish it from traditional approaches to teaching and learning. Explain the relationship between open pedagogy and renewable assignments. Differentiate between disposable and renewable assignments. Explain AI literacy Describe the importance of AI literacy for the responsible use of generative AI tools. Critically reflect on their own experiences using generative AI tools. Learn from the experiences of other students through collaborative activities. Transform personal and shared experiences into AI literacy resources. Collaboratively develop AI literacy resources suitable for open dissemination. Develop AI literacy resources for dissemination through Repositories of AI Literacy Resources (RAILR). Target Audience Level: Undergraduate Adaptable for other levels depending on instructors' teaching goals. Suitable as a standalone module or as an elective Module Outline This module is organised into the following sections: Section 1: Purpose of This Module Section 2: Open Pedagogy: From Disposable Assignments to Shared Knowledge Section 3: Learning from Experience: Why Students' Experiences with Generative AI Tools Matter Section 4: From Reflection to Resource Creation: Transforming Experience into AI Literacy Resources Section 5: Repository-Based Knowledge Sharing: Preserving and Disseminating Student-Created AI Literacy Resources in RAILR Section 6: Reflecting on Your AI Journey: Learning Through Personal Experience Section 7: Practical Learning Activities Practical Activity 1: My AI Journey Practical Activity 2: Learning from Others Practical Activity 3: Co-Creating an AI Literacy Resource Practical Activity 4: Peer Review, Improvement, and Dissemination Practical Activity 5: Complete the Appropriate RAILR Dissemination Agreement Practical Activity 6: Open Dissemination of AI Literacy Resources Section 8. Learning and Reading Resources Assessment Students will complete a series of reflective, collaborative, and resource-development activities. Depending on the instructor's implementation of the module, assessment may include: An individual reflective essay. Participation in collaborative group discussions. Development of a group AI literacy resource. Peer review of another group's AI literacy resource. Preparation of resources for dissemination through RAILR

items.title: PERAN PROGRAM MAKAN BERGIZI GRATIS DALAM MENINGKATKAN MOTIVASI INTRINSIK DAN SEMANGAT BELAJAR PESERTA DIDIK
items.abstract: The implementation of the government’s Makan Bergizi Gratis (MBG) is an example of a policy aimed at improving the quality of human capital by meeting students’ nutritional needsa factor linked to psychological aspects such as intrinsic motivation and enthusiasm for learning. This study specifically examines the role of the MBG Program in enhancing students’ intrinsic motivation and enthusiasm for learning. A quantitative method with a correlational design was applied, involving 220 junior high school students who had participated in the MBG Program and were purposively selected for this study. Data were collected using a questionnaire that covered perceptions of the MBG Program, intrinsic motivation, and enthusiasm for learning, which had undergone validation and reliability testing. The data were statistically analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson’s correlation, and linear regression. The results of the study indicate that the participants’ perceptions of the MBG Program (M = 4.05), intrinsic motivation (M = 3.92), and enthusiasm for learning (M = 3.85) fell into the high category. The MBG Program was positively correlated with students’ intrinsic motivation (r = 0.58) and enthusiasm for learning (r = 0.52), and there was a strong correlation between intrinsic motivation and enthusiasm for learning (r = 0.71). Regression analysis showed that the MBG Program had a significant direct effect on learning enthusiasm (β = 0.21; p = 0.001) and an indirect effect mediated by intrinsic motivation (β = 0.58; p < 0.001), and explained 55.2% of the variance in learning enthusiasm (R² = 0.552). Thus, it can be concluded that the MBG Program is crucial for the development of students’ non-cognitive aspects, both directly and indirectly through the enhancement of intrinsic motivation; therefore, this program warrants the attention of education policymakers.

items.title: PROFESSIONAL-ADAPTIVE MODEL OF TRANSFORMING WOMEN IN UZBEKISTAN FROM AI CONSUMERS TO CREATORS
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing the demand for digital competencies. In particular, the gap between women's level of artificial intelligence usage and their level of independently applying it to create professional and innovative solutions is one of the pressing issues. The purpose of this study is to develop a professional-adaptive AI education model aimed at transitioning women in Uzbekistan from basic users of artificial intelligence to creators of practical solutions. The research utilized methods of system analysis, comparative analysis, model design, and digital educational platform prototyping. The model includes identifying the user's professional field, assessing initial AI competence, forming an individual learning pathway, and providing AI training sessions and practical projects aligned with professional tasks. The SheTechAI platform was developed as a technological prototype of the model. As a result of the research, a four-stage competence model is proposed, aimed at advancing AI education from 'providing knowledge about AI' to 'solving real professional problems and creating new solutions using AI'.

items.title: PSYCHOMETRIC OPERATIONALIZATION OF FUNCTIONAL ROLES IN AUTONOMOUS MULTI-AGENT SYSTEMS BASED ON PERSONAMATRIX: AN AI TRANSITIONAL FIELD FRAMEWORK
items.abstract: Background: Autonomous LLM agents increasingly operate in shared environments where behavior depends on interaction history, role allocation, local norms, authority, and group structure. Objective: This conceptual methods paper develops a psychometric operationalization of dynamic functional roles in autonomous multi-agent systems using PersonaMatrix-derived measurement principles without attributing human psychological ontology to AI. Methods: A targeted evidence synthesis (2019–2026) was conducted across AI psychometrics, dynamic multi-agent roles, collective-field modeling, norm emergence, trajectory prediction, and anthropomorphism. Peer-reviewed sources were prioritized, while current OpenAI, METR/Redwood, Anthropic, and Moltbook materials were used as primary or emerging evidence for recent agent ecosystems. Results: The framework separates output-level stability (RSI, IDS, RCS) from role-level and field-level constructs. It proposes the Functional Role Consistency Index, Role Transition Index, Agent–Field Differentiation Index, Collective Utility Index, Norm Conflict Index, Regulatory Closure Index, and Field Role Composition Vector. Three falsifiable hypotheses test whether role variables add out-of-sample predictive value for agent behavior, role transitions, and future field states. Conclusion: PersonaMatrix is positioned as a measurement architecture rather than an AI personality diagnosis. The archetypal-role hypothesis is supported only if role coding is reliable, improves prediction beyond non-archetypal baselines, and generalizes to unseen agents and independent multi-agent environments.

items.title: Putting AI to the test: Evidence from a large-scale RCT in rural China
items.abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) has heightened interest in personalizing computer assisted learning (CAL) programs to tailor their instruction to individual students. Despite the proliferation of AI-driven CAL programs, evidence for their effectiveness remains limited. We present findings from a field experiment in rural China examining whether an AI-driven personalized CAL program improves student achievement. We randomly assign 8647 students from 315 primary school classes to one of three treatment arms: (i) AI-CAL, (ii) non-personalized CAL (active control), and (iii) non-CAL educational activities (pure control). Results indicate that AI-CAL does not significantly improve achievement, with estimates precise enough to rule out non-trivial positive effects. This finding holds across the difficulty of assessment items and across the baseline achievement of students. If anything, AI-CAL might be less effective than non-personalized CAL for students in the middle tercile of baseline achievement. These findings call for caution when scaling AI-driven educational technologies.
